body.statement: Let \(k,p\geq0\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times p}\).  There is a vector \(\xi^A\) of mutually independent, nonconstant, non-Gaussian, finite-support real random variables such that, for every \(q\geq0\), every \(D\in\mathbb R^{k\times q}\), and every vector \(\eta\) of mutually independent nonconstant real random variables, the equality \(\mathcal L(A\xi^A)=\mathcal L(D\eta)\) implies the existence of a surjection \(f:U_A\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero scalars \(a_i\), \(i\in U_A\), satisfying \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\).  If the coordinates of \(\eta\) are also non-Gaussian, this conclusion remains unchanged.
body.proof_tex:
Let \(F\) be the subfield of \(\mathbb R\) generated by the finitely many entries of \(A\); it is countable.  Put \(U=U_A\).  Choose positive numbers \((r_i)_{i\in U}\) algebraically independent over \(F\).  Such a finite family exists recursively because the elements algebraic over a countable field form a countable set, whereas every nonempty real interval is uncountable.  Set \(h_i=r_iA_{:,i}\).  If \(\sum_{i\in U}m_i h_i=0\) for integers \(m_i\), every coordinate gives a polynomial relation over \(F\) among the \(r_i\)'s.  Algebraic independence implies \(m_iA_{vi}=0\) for every \(v,i\), and the nonzeroness of column \(i\) gives \(m_i=0\).  Hence
\[
 \Lambda=\bigoplus_{i\in U}\mathbb Z h_i                                      \tag{7}
\]
is a free abelian group on the displayed generators.

Choose \(p_i\in(0,1)\), take independent \(Z_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)\), and put \(\xi_i^A=r_iZ_i\) for \(i\in U\).  Give the zero columns independent nonconstant Bernoulli coordinates as well.  These coordinates have finite support and are non-Gaussian.  By (7), the law of \(A\xi^A\) has the \(2^{|U|}\) distinct support points
\[
 \left\{\sum_{i\in U}z_i h_i:z_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.                         \tag{8}
\]

Suppose \(\mathcal L(A\xi^A)=\mathcal L(D\eta)\), and write \(Y_j=D_{:,j}\eta_j\) for \(j\in U_D\).  The support of a convolution contains the Minkowski sum of the supports: if one chooses a support point from each independent summand, every product neighborhood has positive probability and its sum is a neighborhood of the summed point.  Since (8) is finite, fixing support points of all but one \(Y_j\) shows that each \(Y_j\) has finite support.  Moreover, \(Y_j\) is nonconstant because \(D_{:,j}\ne0\) and \(\eta_j\) is nonconstant.

Choose \(y_j^0\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\).  If \(y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), hold all other selected support points fixed and compare the two resulting sums.  Both belong to (8), so \(y-y_j^0\in\Lambda\).  Freeness in (7) gives a unique vector \(\nu_j(y)\in\mathbb Z^U\) with
\[
 y-y_j^0=\sum_{i\in U}\nu_j(y)_i h_i.
\]
Define the finite Laurent polynomial
\[
 F_j(z)=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)}
          \Pr(Y_j=y)z^{\nu_j(y)}.
\]
Independence and equality of the two laws imply coefficient by coefficient, using the injective map from exponent vectors to \(\Lambda\), that
\[
 \prod_{j\in U_D}F_j(z)
 =c z^\gamma\prod_{i\in U}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_i z_i\bigr)                         \tag{9}
\]
for a positive \(c\) and a Laurent monomial \(z^\gamma\).  The proved Laurent-factorization lemma partitions \(U\) into nonempty sets \((I_j)_{j\in U_D}\).  They are nonempty because each \(Y_j\), and hence each \(F_j\), is nonconstant.  If \(i\in I_j\), the product form of \(F_j\) has two support exponents differing by the \(i\)-th coordinate vector.  Thus two support points of \(Y_j\) differ by \(h_i\).  Both points lie on the line \(\mathbb R D_{:,j}\), so
\[
 A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,j}
\]
for some \(a_i\ne0\).  Setting \(f(i)=j\) for \(i\in I_j\) gives the asserted surjection.

If \(U=\varnothing\), the left side is constant.  The same support argument forces every \(Y_j\) to be constant, which contradicts \(j\in U_D\); hence \(U_D=\varnothing\) and the empty map is the required surjection.  The argument imposed no Gaussianity condition on \(\eta\), so it applies in particular when its coordinates are non-Gaussian.
